concepts.title: Series Creation from Scalars, Arrays and Dictionary
concepts.definition: A Pandas Series is a one-dimensional labelled column of values, built either from a list of scalars, from a 1-D NumPy array, or from a dictionary whose keys turn into the labels. Without explicit labels the positions run from 0 through N-1, and when custom labels are supplied their count must equal the value count, otherwise a ValueError reports the length mismatch.
concepts.key_idea: Keys of a dictionary become labels; values and labels must agree in number, and the default labels end at count minus one.
question_patterns: what are the default index values of a series built from 10 values
a series is built from 4 values with only 3 labels; what error does Pandas raise

create a series of 2, 3, 4 labelled Feb, Mar, Apr and state the value at Mar
why must the length of the index match the length of the passed values

solution_steps.explain: default labels run 0 to N-1, so the final one is the value count minus one
4 values against 3 labels differ by 1, which the ValueError message reports

worked_examples.q: A series is built from 4 values but 5 custom labels. What does pandas raise?

concepts.title: Positional versus Labelled Slicing
concepts.definition: Slicing cuts a sub-series out of a series. With positional integers the end position is excluded, so [1:3] hands back only positions 1 and 2; with labels the end label is included, so 'USA':'France' hands back three values. Reversing a series uses a negative step [::-1].
concepts.key_idea: Count a positional cut as end minus start; a labelled cut adds one because the end label stays in.
question_patterns: how many values does seriesCapCntry[1:3] return and which labels do they carry
how many values does seriesCapCntry['USA':'France'] return

solution_steps.explain: positions 1 and 2 survive the cut 1:3 because position 3 is excluded: 3 - 1 = 2 values

solution_steps.action: add one for the labelled cut
solution_steps.explain: USA to France keeps the end label, so the same span returns 2 + 1 = 3 values

concepts.title: Series Arithmetic and NaN Alignment
concepts.definition: Adding or subtracting two series matches values by label, not by position. Only labels present in both series get a numeric result; every label unique to one side lands as NaN in the output, and the output carries the union of all labels. For seriesA and seriesB of the chapter, the union holds 7 labels of which 3 match, so 4 results are NaN.
concepts.key_idea: Matched labels compute (a: 1 + -10 = -9); unmatched labels on either side produce NaN.
question_patterns: how many NaN values appear in seriesA + seriesB for the two five-label series of the chapter
what is the value at label a after seriesA + seriesB
why does the result of adding two unaligned series carry the union of their indexes
which labels of seriesA + seriesB produce NaN and why
find the result at label e when seriesA adds seriesB
does seriesA + seriesB match values by position or by label

solution_steps.explain: 5 labels on each side with 3 shared give 5 + 5 - 3 = 7 output labels
only the 3 matched labels compute, so 7 - 3 = 4 results are NaN

worked_examples.q: Two series share 3 labels and their union holds 7. How many NaN results appear when they are added?

concepts.title: fill_value Methods: add, sub, mul, div
concepts.definition: The explicit methods add(), sub(), mul() and div() do the same arithmetic as the operators but accept a fill_value that stands in for a missing side before computing. With fill_value=1000, the label b of seriesA.sub(seriesB) becomes 2 - 1000 = -998, and the label y becomes 1000 - 20 = 980, replacing what would have been NaN.
concepts.key_idea: Where one side is missing, the fill steps in for it; the arithmetic then proceeds label by label.
question_patterns: what does seriesA.sub(seriesB, fill_value=1000) return at label b
compute the result at label y for seriesA.sub(seriesB, fill_value=1000)
why do the methods add(), sub(), mul() and div() prefer fill_value over plain operators
what does seriesA.add(seriesB, fill_value=0) return at label d
which value fills the missing side before a sub() with fill_value=1000 at label z
how does div() with fill_value=0 behave at labels where seriesB is missing

solution_steps.action: fill the missing side of label y
solution_steps.explain: seriesA lacks y, so the fill 1000 substitutes for it: 1000 - 20 = 980

solution_steps.action: fill the missing side of label b
solution_steps.explain: seriesB lacks b, so the fill substitutes there: 2 - 1000 = -998

worked_examples.q: With fill_value=1000, seriesA.sub(seriesB) at a label where A has 2 and B lacks the label gives what?

concepts.title: DataFrame from Dictionary of Lists and Series
concepts.definition: A DataFrame grows naturally out of dictionaries: dictionary keys become the column labels and the lists (or series) become the rows or columns. When several series with different labels build one DataFrame, the row labels become the union of all series indexes, and every label a series lacks turns into a NaN cell.
concepts.key_idea: Keys become columns, label unions become rows, and each absent label-value pair is stored as NaN.
question_patterns: how are the keys of a dictionary used when creating a DataFrame

solution_steps.action: count what each column is missing
solution_steps.explain: each series holds 5 of the 7 union labels, so it misses 7 - 5 = 2 labels
2 missing labels per column across 3 columns gives 6 NaN cells, exactly as the chapter output shows

worked_examples.q: Dictionary keys become the what of a DataFrame: columns or rows?

concepts.title: DataFrame Attributes: shape, size, T
concepts.definition: A DataFrame reports its geometry through attributes: shape returns the (rows, columns) tuple, size returns the total cell count (their product), index and columns list the labels, dtypes gives each column's type, values strips the labels into an ndarray, and T flips the frame so rows and columns trade places.
concepts.key_idea: Size equals rows times columns; appending one column adds exactly one cell per row.
question_patterns: what do ForestAreaDF.shape and ForestAreaDF.size return

solution_steps.explain: 4 rows by 3 columns give the size 12 shown for ForestAreaDF
a new column contributes one cell per existing row: 12 + 4 = 16 cells

concepts.title: Adding and Dropping Rows and Columns
concepts.definition: Assigning to a fresh column label appends a column at the end, while an existing label updates that column; loc[ ] adds or rewrites whole rows by label. The drop() method removes rows with axis=0 and columns with axis=1, deleting every row that shares a duplicated label, and shrinkage in cells can be tracked arithmetically.
concepts.key_idea: New label means add, existing label means update; each dropped column removes one cell per remaining row.
question_patterns: write the statement to add a column Preeti with marks 89, 78, 76 to ResultDF

solution_steps.explain: dropping 3 of the 5 columns removes 3 cells per row: 15 - 3 * 3 = 6 cells remain

worked_examples.q: Which axis value does drop() use to remove columns?

concepts.title: append Method for DataFrames
concepts.definition: The append() method stacks the rows of a second DataFrame after the first, inventing NaN where columns do not line up and adding unseen columns on the fly. Setting ignore_index=True discards the old row labels and numbers the stacked rows from zero, while verify_integrity=True raises an error on duplicate labels.
concepts.key_idea: Rows stack end to end; with ignore_index the combined rows are relabelled 0 through total rows minus one.
question_patterns: how many rows result when a 3-row DataFrame is appended to another 3-row DataFrame

solution_steps.explain: 3 rows plus 3 rows give 6 rows in the appended frame
ignore_index numbers rows from 0, so the final label is 6 - 1 = 5

worked_examples.q: Which append() setting renumbers the stacked rows from zero?

concepts.title: CSV Import Export and Series versus ndarray
concepts.definition: read_csv() loads a comma separated file into a DataFrame, with sep choosing the delimiter, header naming the row that supplies column labels and names supplying fresh ones; to_csv() writes a DataFrame back out, where header=False and index=False suppress the column and row labels. Unlike NumPy arrays, series align by label during operations, tolerate NaN for missing matches, allow non-unique and descending labels, but cost more memory.
concepts.key_idea: Keys and headers shape the frame on the way in; header=False and index=False slim the file on the way out; series align by label while ndarrays do not.
question_patterns: which parameter of read_csv() decides the row used as column names
write the statement to save a DataFrame without row labels or column headers
which parameter of read_csv() supplies fresh column labels
state two differences between a Pandas series and a NumPy ndarray
how do unaligned series behave compared to unaligned ndarrays during an operation
which separator character does the to_csv example use to write resultonly.txt

solution_steps.explain: sep fixes the delimiter, header=0 takes labels from the first line, names overrides them
header=False drops column names from the file and index=False drops the row labels
series align on labels and fill gaps with NaN; ndarrays have fixed positional indexing and no NaN alignment
